title: THE WOMAN DAVID COULDN’T HAVE: Bathsheba, Power, Adultery, and Murder
paragraphs: THE WOMAN DAVID COULDN’T HAVE: Bathsheba, Power, Adultery, and Murder

He had defeated giants, survived assassins, conquered kingdoms, and become Israel’s celebrated king. But one evening, David reached for the one thing God had not given him—and before the story was over, a marriage had been violated, a faithful soldier was dead, a child would die, and the man after God’s own heart would discover that no throne is high enough to hide sin from the eyes of God.
There is a sentence near the end of 2 Samuel 11 that should terrify anyone who has ever become comfortable with secret sin.
David thought the matter was finished.
Bathsheba was brought into David’s house.
The pregnancy could now appear legitimate.
The battlefield could absorb the questions.
The palace could control the story.
And then Scripture gives us God’s version of events:
וַיֵּרַע הַדָּבָר אֲשֶׁר־עָשָׂה דָוִד בְּעֵינֵי יְהוָה
Vayyeraʿ haddavar asher-asah David beʿenei YHWH.
“The thing David had done was evil in the eyes of the LORD.”
That is the sentence David could not silence.
Because you can control what people hear about you.
You can smile in church while something inside you is rotting.
But you cannot edit what God saw.
And that is where this story becomes uncomfortable.
Because this is not merely a story about David.
It is about what happens when desire is given permission to become entitlement.
It is about what happens when someone blessed by God begins believing that blessing means everything he wants must belong to him.
It is about the frightening distance between being used by God and walking closely with God.
And ultimately, it is about something even greater.
It is about a King who failed...
and another King who came through David’s bloodline to save failures like him.
But before we reach grace, Scripture makes us walk through the scandal.
David was not an obscure man trying to find his place in the world.
He had already been given more than most men could dream of possessing.
He had known the presence of God.
He had written songs of worship.
He had wealth, authority, soldiers, servants, wives, influence, and a name people would remember for thousands of years.
Yet 2 Samuel 11 begins with a strangely ominous detail.
It was the season “when kings go out to battle.”
The king who had once run toward a giant was now lingering at home while other men fought his battles.
David rose from his bed and walked along the roof of the palace.
Scripture describes her as extraordinarily beautiful.
And the answer should have ended everything.
“Is this not Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite?”
Bathsheba, daughter of Eliam, wife of Uriah the Hittite.
And the Hebrew narration becomes chillingly economical.
The biblical narrator places the initiative unmistakably with David. He is the king. He sees. He investigates. He sends. He takes. Then the text says she came to him and he lay with her.

We should be careful not to claim details Scripture does not explicitly give us. The passage does not provide a transcript of Bathsheba’s thoughts, nor does it narrate the encounter in enough detail for us to reconstruct every question modern readers may ask about her agency or consent.
But Scripture leaves absolutely no ambiguity about who possessed the power and who drove the sequence of events.
This was not simply a lonely shepherd boy falling unexpectedly into temptation.
This was Israel’s king using royal power to obtain another man’s wife.
And sometimes sin begins exactly there.
Not when you see something beautiful.
But when you decide that wanting something gives you the right to have it.
There are things you can desire that you must never touch.
There are relationships you must never enter.
There are conversations you must end.
There are messages you must not send.
There are doors you must not open.
There are fantasies you must stop feeding.
Because God knows what uncontrolled desire eventually devours.
And perhaps David imagined that the moment would disappear into history.
Except sin has an ancient habit of sending invoices after the pleasure is gone.
A message came back from Bathsheba.
Only two words are needed in Hebrew:
And this is where the story becomes terrifyingly relatable.
Because many people do not destroy their lives with the first sin.
They destroy their lives trying to hide it.
David summoned Uriah from the battlefield.
Let him sleep with his wife.
Let everyone assume the child is his.
Except Uriah refused to go home.
Because his fellow soldiers were sleeping in the open field.
How could he enjoy the comforts of marriage while they remained exposed?
The Hittite soldier demonstrated the loyalty that Israel’s anointed king had abandoned.
Still Uriah would not go home.
And now David’s sin needed something darker.
David wrote a letter to Joab ordering Uriah to be placed where the fighting was fiercest and then abandoned so that he would be struck down.
And David did something almost unimaginably cold.
He placed Uriah’s death sentence into Uriah’s own hands.
Uriah carried the letter back to the battlefield.
The faithful soldier unknowingly delivered the instructions for his own execution.
Other soldiers died in the operation too.
That is another thing sin rarely tells you beforehand.
It almost never stays contained to the person who commits it.
Your secret can bleed into somebody else’s life.
Your compromise can wound your spouse.
Your addiction can reshape your children.
Your bitterness can poison your home.
Your hidden double life can devastate people who never consented to participate in it.
That may be one of the most dangerous moments in the entire story.
Because consequences do not always arrive immediately.
Sometimes you can sin and still go to work tomorrow.
Still have people call you blessed.
And the absence of immediate judgment can seduce a person into believing God did not notice.
After the mourning period, David brought her into his house.
She gave birth to a son.
From the outside, perhaps the scandal had been successfully rewritten.
But David was not the only storyteller.
Nathan did not begin by screaming accusations.
There was a rich man with many sheep.
Nearby lived a poor man who owned only one little ewe lamb.
That lamb was precious to him.
It was like a daughter to him.
Then a traveler arrived at the rich man’s house.
Instead of taking one of his own many animals, the rich man seized the poor man’s only lamb and prepared it for his guest.
The former shepherd understood exactly how monstrous the act was.
How could anyone do something so heartless?
And then Nathan looked at the king.
Imagine the silence after those words.
David had been furious at a sinner...
without realizing he was describing himself.
And perhaps that is why this story reaches across three thousand years and puts its hand on our shoulder.
Because we are often brilliant at identifying sin from the spectator’s seat.
And we become Nathan in everybody else’s story while refusing to hear Nathan in our own.
But sooner or later, God’s Word turns toward us.
This is not about your neighbor anymore.
Not the pastor who disappointed you.
Not the celebrity whose scandal entertained you.
That does not mean we have all committed David’s particular sins.
It means none of us escapes the deeper diagnosis of Scripture: sin is not merely something happening somewhere out there.
It lives frighteningly close to home.
No blaming the pressures of leadership.
Not with “There were circumstances you don’t understand.”
Not with “I’m sorry you were offended.”
Psalm 51 has traditionally been received as David’s prayer in connection with this sin, and its language is devastating because David does not ask God to polish his reputation.
He asks God to cleanse him.
“Create in me a clean heart, O God.”
He understood something we desperately need to recover.
The greatest problem was not that David had damaged his image.
The greatest problem was that David had sinned against the holy God.
this is where the Gospel begins glowing through the wreckage.
But forgiveness did not mean pretending nothing happened.
Scripture never teaches that grace makes evil harmless.
Forgiveness removes condemnation before God for the repentant believer because of His mercy; it does not magically erase every earthly consequence our choices create.
Grace is not God calling darkness light.
Grace is God entering the darkness to rescue sinners from what they have become.
And then comes one of the most astonishing details in the Bible.
Then Matthew opens his Gospel with the genealogy of Jesus Christ.
He could have written Bathsheba’s name.
Δαυὶδ δὲ ἐγέννησεν τὸν Σολομῶνα ἐκ τῆς τοῦ Οὐρίου
David de egennēsen ton Solomōna ek tēs tou Ouriou.
David fathered Solomon “by the [woman] of Uriah.”
The Bible refuses to sanitize David’s history.
Matthew does not airbrush the genealogy of Jesus.
The genealogy does not say sin did not matter.
It shows us something far greater.
Human sin could not stop God’s redemptive purpose.
Out of a family line containing sexual sin, violence, brokenness, outsiders, failures, kings, widows, scandals, and graves came the spotless Son of God.
Not because God approved of the evil.
Because evil does not get the final word when God writes the ending.
Jesus came to rescue His bride.
David sent an innocent man to die to protect himself.
Jesus willingly went to death to save the guilty.
Jesus, though Lord of all, humbled Himself and gave Himself for sinners.
David tried to cover his sin with another man’s blood.
Jesus covers repentant sinners with His own.
That is the difference between the kingdom of fallen man and the Kingdom of Christ.
One king says, “You die so I can keep what I want.”
The other King says, “I will die so you can be made new.”
And maybe that is why you have read this far.
Maybe there is something you have been hiding.
Money you should never have taken.
A marriage you are quietly destroying.
A private life that looks nothing like the Christian life people believe you have.
You have been trying to manage it.
But it also means hiding is unnecessary.
Because the God who exposed David was also the God to whom David could return.
The answer is not to become better at concealment.
Call sin what God calls it.
Where appropriate, confess to those you have wronged and seek to make things right.
Seek wise pastoral help and accountability when needed.
Not after you have cleaned yourself.
The Gospel is not that good people receive Jesus as their reward.
The Gospel is that sinners who could never save themselves are offered forgiveness and reconciliation with God through the crucified and risen Christ.
Jesus does not rewrite everything by pretending the old chapters never happened.
He rewrites everything by refusing to let sin have the final chapter.
That is why the cross matters.
At Calvary, God did not shrug at evil.
Sin was so serious that the Son of God bore judgment.
And grace was so astonishing that He willingly did it for sinners.
Maybe you feel more like David than you ever wanted to admit.
And Jesus changes what “the end” means.
You cannot buy blessing, forgiveness, salvation, or greater standing before God.
But you can choose to support Gospel-centered work that you believe is worth helping continue.

If glorifying God is your desire, let that desire become more than a feeling. Glorify Him in repentance. Glorify Him in obedience. Glorify Him by sharing biblical truth. Glorify Him by helping other people hear about Christ.
If you want to support the mission and continue walking with us:
Send it privately to the believer who thinks God could never want them back.
Even invite the unbeliever who thinks Christianity is about pretending Christians never fail.
The Bible does not hide its heroes’ scars.
It points beyond them to the Savior.
And perhaps the person who most needs this article tonight is the person who believes their worst chapter has already determined their ending.
Tell them Scripture remembered the bloodshed.
The King who never abuses His authority.
The King who does not steal another man’s bride but gives His life for His own.
The King who knows every secret before confession ever reaches our lips.
The King who calls sinners out of darkness rather than teaching them how to decorate it.
The King whose grace is greater than our scandal.
Because one evening David looked from his rooftop and believed that because he was king, he could take what belonged to another man.
Centuries later, Jesus Christ looked upon sinners who belonged under judgment...
and instead of taking from them,
So bring Him the chapter you wish you could erase.
Bring Him the thing you cannot undo.
Because the most unforgettable truth in David’s darkest chapter is not that a great man fell.
It is that the greater Son of David eventually came for fallen people.
And when your sin whispers, “This is how your story ends,” remember the bloodstained genealogy that leads all the way to Bethlehem, all the way to Calvary, and all the way to an empty tomb:
Jesus is still writing where shame put a period.
